2018_120_041718regmtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of April 17, 2018 at the Services Building. There are no business items — the substance is a report and an amendment. Budget Amendment #2 raises the 2017-18 General Fund appropriation to $150,661,687 on $1,775,565 of added revenue, and the Facilities Study Team's Attendance Area Review Committee reports on the district's split learning pathways and overcrowding, with final recommendations aimed at 2019-2020. The packet also carries the March 20 minutes, which record that all three Section 1 property resolutions and both Early Childhood Center resolutions passed 4-2 over Gottlieb's and Hammond's objections, and recognizes 39 nominees for the Outstanding Teacher Award.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, April 17, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment marks April as Autism Acceptance Month, presented by Barnard Elementary principal Melanie Morey under the banner "Light it Up with Kindness." The district runs autism support classrooms at Barnard (2), Costello and Leonard at the elementary level, Boulan Park at the middle level, Athens at the high school level, and the Troy Center for Transition post-secondary, with Morse and a new program to be determined. April activities include a "Light it Up Blue" day where students may have one fingernail painted blue with a take-home sheet explaining why — the point being to prompt questions from people outside school — sensitivity training for general education peers, a "Walk a Mile in our shoes" challenge for staff to spend time in an autism classroom, and an Autism Speaks bracelet fundraiser run by student council.

The Board then recognizes **39 individuals nominated for the Troy School District Outstanding Teacher Award**, noting more nominations submitted by former and current students than ever before. Thirty-six receive certificates; three were sent to Oakland Schools for the county-wide program: Katy Stanley (math and social studies, Larson) as TSD Middle School Teacher of the Year, Stacie Klumpp (math, Athens) as TSD High School Teacher of the Year, and **Ed Segovia (2nd grade, Morse) as both TSD Elementary Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year**.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the March 6 workshop, the March 20 regular meeting, the March 22 Board retreat and the March 27 special workshop, plus the February 2018 Treasurer's Report and Budget Amendment #2. (The agenda index labels the treasurer's item "March 2018"; the consent page and the register itself are February.)

**How the March 20 votes actually went**
The minutes carried here show a Board that split. Public communication ran heavily to the Section 1 property — Chris Bunch of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, former Troy trustee Ida Edmunds, and residents Harry Broomfield, Donald Drife, Elizabeth Borrow, Tina Catron and Royal Oak's Mary Bogush all spoke on preservation. Mr. Miletti was absent; President Schmidt relayed that Miletti had asked him to say he fully supported all three Section 1 resolutions. Dr. Philippart, Mrs. Fleming and Mr. Hauff said they would support them; Mrs. Hammond was **not in favor of deeding the land to a conservancy**; Mr. Gottlieb said the information received was inaccurate and **recommended tabling**.

| Resolution | Vote |
| --- | --- |
| 18-029 Section 16 purchase agreement ($3,383,000.00) | 6-0 |
| 18-030 Section 1 division of parcel | 4-2 |
| 18-031 Section 1 preservation of Parent Parcel | 4-2 |
| 18-032 Section 1 RFP, front parcel only | 4-2 |
| 18-033 network equipment, Presidio $1,847,628.40 | 6-0 |
| 18-034 musical instruments etc., $393,635.73 | 6-0 |
| 18-035 Early Childhood Center financing, $11,000,000 | 4-2 |
| 18-036 Early Childhood Center construction, $17,963,193.15 | 4-2 |

Every 4-2 was Fleming, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt in favor, Gottlieb and Hammond opposed, Miletti absent.

**Treasurer's Report — February 2018**
Total check disbursements are $7,644,226.17, with the General Fund group at $6,812,415.61 and the General Fund (101) itself at $6,500,187.79. Adding $1,941,942.09 of wire transfers, $183,094.71 of P-Card purchases and $19,865.79 of ACH debits, less $2,154.60 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $9,786,974.16. The Early Childhood Center Fund (531) appears in the fund breakdown for the first time, at $3,715.00. General Fund balance at February 28, 2018 is $19,162,931.

**Budget Amendment #2**
The 2017-18 amendment covers the General Fund (Amendment 2), Food Service, Troy Career Center, Adult Education and Community Service, Capital Projects and Capital Maintenance (each Amendment 1), plus the budget adoption for the new Early Childhood Learning Center Fund. Amended appropriations: **General Fund $150,661,687**, Capital Projects $35,949,281, Capital Maintenance $6,345,557, Adult Education and Community Service $4,043,585, Food Service $3,696,036, Troy Career Center $2,520,823 and Early Childhood Learning Center $2,421,731.

General Fund revenue rises $1,775,565 to $151,448,471 — state up $557,801 to $101,615,237, federal up $547,224 to $3,997,995, incoming transfers and other up $474,540 to $7,955,485, local up $196,000 to $37,879,754 — against an unchanged July 1 fund balance of $24,205,391, for $175,653,862 total available to appropriate. On the spending side, instruction rises $1,252,192 to $103,891,055 and support services $758,656 to $46,592,740, with the largest single swing a **$1,314,235 reduction in general administration** to $1,028,661, offset by increases of $918,281 in instructional staff and $778,628 in central services.

**Curriculum — the attendance area review**
Dr. Machesky summarizes the Facilities Study Team – Attendance Area Review Committee report first given at the April 10 workshop. The committee's charge was to resolve double split learning pathways, examine enrollment across buildings to address inappropriate overcrowding and imbalances, and minimize changes to attendance areas. It met on Monday evenings from October 16, 2017 to March 12, 2018 — **15 hours of meeting time excluding site visits** to Smith, Larson, Barnard, Costello and Hill.

The pathway problem has three shapes: a **double switch**, where Troy Union students split between Smith and Larson and the Smith group splits again to Athens; a **single switch**, where Wattles and Morse students at Baker split between Troy High and Athens; and a **middle school switch**, where Hamilton students split between Smith and Boulan Park but reconverge at Troy High. Five concerns are named — the Emerald Lakes quadrant double split from Troy Union, overcrowding at Barnard, at Schroeder and Bemis, and at Boulan Park, and the Hamilton feeder path. The report's own verdict on the constraints — geography, distance limitations, residential development, pathway retention, middle and high school imbalances — is blunt: "No Elegant Solution!"

Next steps send multiple options to transportation for cost estimates while central office examines Schools of Choice draw-down at specific schools, actual fall 2018 enrollment, potential grandfathering based on past practice and additional "neighborhood adjacent" options, with **final recommendations to be considered for implementation in 2019-2020**.

**Personnel**
A probationary contract for Lauren DeGrazia, .8 social worker at Barnard Elementary.

A note on the treasurer's item: the agenda index reads "Treasurer's Report - March 2018," while the consent agenda page and the underlying register are for February 2018. The February labelling is the one the documents themselves carry.

**Recognition 2.A: oneTROY autism programming.** The Mission Moment highlights the district's autism programs, April being designated Autism Awareness Month. The introduction describes autism as a condition characterized by difficulty in communicating and forming relationships, with students challenged in their ability to recognize and understand the thoughts, beliefs, desires and intentions of other people in order to make sense of their behavior and predict what they are going to do. Melanie Morey, principal of Barnard Elementary School, presents; the item is for recognition only and no certificates are handed out.

The presentation is titled "Troy School District celebrates Autism Acceptance Month — Light it Up with Kindness!" Its facts slide describes Autism Spectrum Disorder as a neurobiological disorder that typically affects development within the first three years of life, characterized by impaired communication ability (which may be verbal, partially verbal or non-verbal); impaired social interaction; restricted and/or repetitive interests and behaviors, including repetitive actions and verbally repeating words, phrases or sentences; and sensory issues involving over- or under-stimulation.

Autism support classrooms in the district are listed as Barnard (2), Costello and Leonard at the elementary level, with Morse and a new program to be determined; Boulan Park at the middle school level; Athens at the high school level; and the Troy Center for Transition post-secondary.

During April, schools around the district celebrate autism, and the framing is deliberate: the district is celebrating Autism ACCEPTANCE, moving past awareness to promote a culture of acceptance within the school community. Activities for students include a "Light it Up Blue" day, on which students may have one fingernail painted blue and receive a small take-home sheet explaining the purpose — the idea being to get people outside the school asking about the painted fingernail so students can talk to them about autism acceptance — encouragement to wear blue, "Light it Up with Kindness" lessons for teachers to share throughout the week, and sensitivity training for general education peers. For staff there is a "Walk a Mile in our shoes" challenge to spend time in an autism classroom to better understand how to support students with special needs in their own classrooms, a kickoff breakfast thanking staff for creating a culture of acceptance, and building-wide professional development on the spectrum of differentiation and universal supports for all students. For the community, student council sells autism awareness bracelets through the month with proceeds going toward the Autism Speaks walk that summer, which families and staff are encouraged to join. The closing slide notes that creating a culture of acceptance does not stop in April, and that the peer-to-peer programs continue to serve as a way for students to promote that culture throughout OneTroy.

**Recognition 2.B: Oakland County Outstanding Teacher of the Year awards.** The Board recognizes the accomplishments of 39 individuals nominated for the Troy School District Outstanding Teacher Award Program. The nominees represent exemplary educators at the elementary, middle and high school levels, nominated by peers and parents, and the item notes that this year the district received more nominations than ever submitted by former and current students. Nomination letters described how the professionals honored go above and beyond to ensure their students learn, grow and thrive.

Thirty-six nominees receive certificates and plants: Karen Bush (Schroeder), Colleen Calandra (Hamilton), Sharon Callas (Costello), Kathy Cappuso (Larson), Jason Cichowicz (Schroeder), Erica Conklin (Barnard), Lauren Cooper (Morse), Lindsey DeCourval (Barnard), Jaime Dobronos (Schroeder), Anne Drogosch (Smith), Lauren Fragomeni (Wass), Rhona Gorosh (Bemis), Dustin Harnish (Baker), Bill Hevel (Troy High), Sara Jozefiak (Barnard), Elliot Kern (Bemis), Andrew LaTorre (Baker), Zach MacIntosh (Baker), Carolyn Maher (Wass), Julie Marjamaa (Costello), Terri McCormick (Smith), Judy Morgan (Baker), Amanda Morton (Barnard), Lynn Mui (Wattles), Vivek Nayak (Smith), Tammy Polena (Schroeder), Sara Provost (Hamilton), Dr. Karen Reese (Costello), Michael Reimann (Smith), Bahia Rouvalis (Martell), Cathy Rozmanik (Costello), Christine Russell (Hamilton), Theresa Schwarz (Wass), Margaret Slankster (Troy High), Valerie Valentino (Troy High) and Staci Vought (Athens).

Three district nominees were sent to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the county-wide outstanding teacher award program: Katy Stanley, math and social studies teacher at Larson Middle School, named TSD Middle School Teacher of the Year; Stacie Klumpp, math teacher at Athens High School, named TSD High School Teacher of the Year; and Ed Segovia, second grade teacher at Morse Elementary, named both TSD Elementary Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year. All three are invited to say a few words.

**Consent minutes: the March 6 workshop.** President Schmidt called the workshop to order at 6:00 p.m. with Mrs. Fleming absent and approximately 10 members in the audience. Public communication came from Mrs. Ida Edmunds on the Section 1 district-owned property and Mr. Chris Bunch of Six Rivers Land Conservancy on the same. The business services update covered the property discussion — Section 16 purchase agreement and Section 1 — wireless network and switches, musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies, a custodial contract addendum, and the Early Childhood Center's construction and financing. The workshop adjourned at 9:40 p.m., a nearly four-hour session on the eve of the March 20 votes.

**Consent minutes: the March 20, 2018 regular meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart were present; Mr. Miletti was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky, administrators Birmingham, Carson, Griffor, Harris, Jansen, Duda, Recker, Soggs, Kwasny and West, and approximately 120 members of the audience.

The Board recognized the students and staff at Troy High, Athens, Boulan Park and Larson who reached out to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, and honored Larson Middle School as a 2018 State School of Character with Wass Elementary as an Honorable Mention school.

Public communication was dominated by the Section 1 property. Chris Bunch of Six Rivers Land Conservancy addressed the Board regarding it; Ida Edmunds, a Troy resident and former Troy Board trustee, spoke on preservation of the Section 1 property; and so did Harry Broomfield of 6301 Evanswood, Donald Drife of 1813 Beech Lane, Mary Bogush of 1418 Ottawa in Royal Oak, Elizabeth Borrow of 2636 Robart and Tina Catron of 2385 Topaz.

Resolution 18-028 approved the consent agenda 6-0 with Miletti absent. Resolution 18-029 adopted the Section 16 purchase agreement, accepting Mondrian Properties' offer of $3,383,000.00 with a $25,000.00 earnest money deposit for the 19.43 +/- acres at Sidwell 20-16-401-002, carried 6-0 with Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt in favor and Miletti absent.

Before the Section 1 votes, Mr. Schmidt provided an overview of the three resolutions to be presented that evening, noting that they are all tied to each other, and gave each member an opportunity to weigh in: whether the Board wants to subdivide and separate the 7 acres of frontage; whether it wants to preserve the land in the back by deeding it to a land conservancy; and whether it wants to market the front 7 acres for sale. Dr. Philippart said she would vote in favor of all three. Mrs. Hammond was not in favor of deeding the land to a conservancy. Mrs. Fleming said she would support the resolutions, as did Mr. Hauff. Mr. Gottlieb recommended tabling them. President Schmidt relayed that although Mr. Miletti could not attend, Miletti had asked him to share that he fully supported all three Section 1 resolutions. Mr. Schmidt then gave a brief history of all district-owned property the Board had been examining over the previous three years and shared information about Section 1 provided by the DEQ, consultants and appraisers, before saying he would support the resolutions and asking for a motion.

Resolution 18-030 authorized the division of the 80 +/- acre Section 1 property into a 7.69 +/- acre parcel fronting Square Lake Road and a remainder Parent Parcel. Mrs. Hammond indicated she did not agree with the proposed split and did not support the resolution; Mr. Gottlieb said that in his opinion the information received is inaccurate and he did not support it. The vote was 4 yes (Fleming, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt), 2 no (Gottlieb, Hammond), Miletti absent. Resolution 18-031, preservation of the Parent Parcel — maintaining it in perpetuity in its natural and undeveloped condition, reserving the district's authority to sell wetlands mitigation credits, negotiating a conservation easement with the MDEQ or a land conservancy and conveying the parcel with an estimated $150,000 of seed money — carried on the same 4-2 split. Resolution 18-032, authorizing an RFP toward the sale of the 7.69 +/- acre front parcel, also carried 4-2 on the same division.

Resolution 18-033 awarded the network equipment to Presidio in the amount of $1,847,628.40 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, carried 6-0. Resolution 18-034 awarded the musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies at $393,635.73 — Dick Blick $29,979.00, Evola Music $18,220.00, K & S Music $960.00, Lone Star Percussion $2,839.63, Music & Arts $15,423.20, Marshall Music $92,349.50, Sam Ash Music $13,311.00, Washington Music Center $186,732.40, Wenger Corporation $27,819.00 and Woodwind & Brasswind $6,002.00 — carried 6-0.

Resolution 18-035 adopted the Early Childhood Center financing resolution authorizing not more than $11,000,000 of bonds under Section 1351(2) of Act 451 without a vote of the school electors, carried 4-2 with Gottlieb and Hammond opposed. Resolution 18-036 awarded bid 9855 for Early Childhood Center construction at $17,963,193.15, likewise 4-2. The pattern is consistent across the evening: the two equipment awards and the land sale were unanimous among those present, while everything touching the Section 1 land disposition and the early childhood project drew the same two dissents.

**Consent minutes: the March 22 retreat and March 27 special workshop.** The March 22 retreat began at 6:02 p.m. with Dr. Philippart absent and no one in the audience; administrators Dziatczak, Griffor, Harris, Trotter and West attended along with business office accountant LaTisha Goulbourne. The agenda was a budget update covering 2018-19 financial planning and Budget Amendment #2, adjourning at 7:42 p.m. The March 27 special workshop began at 6:05 p.m. with all seven members present, Superintendent Machesky, administrator Jordan Harris and Human Resources Consultant Larry Lobert, and no one in the audience; the agenda was board professional learning — a team assessment review and discussion — adjourning at 9:15 p.m.

**Consent item 5.F: the 2017-18 Budget Amendment Resolution.** The amendment covers the General Fund (Amendment 2), the Food Service Fund (Amendment 1), the Troy Career Center (Amendment 1), the Adult Education and Community Service Fund (Amendment 1), the Capital Projects Funds (Amendment 1), the Capital Maintenance Fund (Amendment 1), and the budget adoption for the Early Childhood Learning Center Fund — the first appropriation for the fund created to build and run the new preschool. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. The resolution amends and approves the general appropriations and budget of the Troy School District for fiscal year 2017-18 for those funds as attached and made part of the official minutes of the April 17, 2018 regular meeting.

The amended fund totals are: General Fund $150,661,687; Food Service Fund $3,696,036; Troy Career Center Fund $2,520,823; Adult Education and Community Service Fund $4,043,585; Capital Projects Fund $35,949,281; Capital Maintenance Fund $6,345,557; and Early Childhood Learning Center Fund $2,421,731.

On the General Fund revenue side, the resolution restates the total revenues and unappropriated fund balance estimated to be available for appropriation, comparing the proposed budget to the amended budget: local revenue $37,683,754 to $37,879,754, a change of $196,000; state revenue $101,057,436 to $101,615,237, up $557,801; federal revenue $3,450,771 to $3,997,995, up $547,224; and incoming transfers and other $7,480,945 to $7,955,485, up $474,540. **Personnel 6.A: elementary and secondary.** The Board is recommended to approve a probationary contract for the 2017-2018 school year for Lauren DeGrazia, .8 social worker at Barnard Elementary. Her biographical sketch records a B.A. in human services from Finlandia University, Hancock, Michigan, June 2004, and a Master of Social Work from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, specializing in interpersonal practice with children and youth in families and society, licensed June 2009; her experience is with Total Education Solutions as a contracted school social worker from August 2016 to November 2017, Wayne Westland Community Schools as a social worker from April 2012 to November 2015, and Clara B. Ford Academy in Dearborn Heights from July 2010 to April 2012. She resides in Madison Heights.

**Curriculum 7.A: attendance area review summary.** Dr. Machesky provides a brief summary of the report shared with the Board at the April 10 Board Workshop. The presentation is from the Facilities Study Team – Attendance Area Review Committee, with Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor as administrative liaisons. Committee members named are Jeff Frederick, Courtney Spangler, Victoria King, Lori Bluhm, Lori Sisk, Emily Cremers, Laura Duzey, Veronica Pala and Delia Rodi-Barczys.

The committee's charge was to conduct a review of current Troy School District attendance area patterns according to specific criteria and present options to the Superintendent: resolve double split learning pathways in Troy; examine enrollment across buildings to address inappropriate overcrowding and inappropriate imbalances; and minimize changes to school attendance areas across Troy.

The timeline runs from calls to the community to serve on the committee in spring and August 2017, selection of team members in September 2017, an initial meeting on October 16, 2017 with identification of necessary resources and an initial request for reports, then meetings on various Monday evenings from 6:00 to 7:30 through March 12, 2018 — a total meeting time of 15 hours excluding visits — with visits to Smith, Larson, Barnard, Costello and Hill on November 16, 2017, and finalization of recommendations and considerations for presentation on March 12, 2018.

The attendance area problem is set out as three kinds of split. A double switch: Troy Union Elementary students split between Smith and Larson Middle Schools, and the Smith Middle School students split again to Athens High School. A single switch: Wattles and Morse Elementary students attending Baker Middle School are split between Troy High and Athens. And a middle school switch: Hamilton Elementary students split between Smith and Boulan Park Middle Schools and then both go to Troy High. The full pathway table is: Troy Union–Larson–Athens; Troy Union–Smith–Athens; Wass–Larson–Athens; Hill–Larson–Athens; Costello–Larson–Athens; Barnard–Baker–Athens; Morse–Baker–Athens; Morse–Baker–Troy; Wattles–Baker–Athens; Wattles–Baker–Troy; Martell–Smith–Troy; Leonard–Smith–Troy; Hamilton–Smith–Troy; Hamilton–Boulan–Troy; Schroeder–Boulan–Troy; and Bemis–Boulan–Troy.

The research inputs were current, historical and future enrollment; on-site visits; pre-school sites; the 2016 FST report; Schools of Choice and non-resident decisions; locker capacity; current capacity; room utilization; development; population density; open enrollment applications; and apartment pathways.

Five key attendance area concerns are identified: the Emerald Lakes quadrant, to eliminate the double split pathway from Troy Union; Barnard overcrowding, considering space at nearby schools to accommodate students; Schroeder and Bemis overcrowding, likewise; Boulan Park Middle School overcrowding, likewise; and the Hamilton feeder path, considering sending students to one middle school. The key conditions constraining any fix are middle school imbalances, high school imbalances, geography including distance limitations and neighboring options, residential development, and pathway retention — under a slide reading "No Elegant Solution!"

The committee describes its method as an iterative process: developing potential recommendations according to the charge criteria, requesting the data necessary to determine future impact on school enrollment, analyzing results against the charge criteria, and rejecting options that fail to satisfy them. Its summary is that it provided initial, potential options to the Superintendent that meet the charge criteria, considered the construction of the Early Childhood Center and program location changes, recognized new residential development in Troy, and recommended optimal solutions based on collaborative research and analysis.

Next steps: multiple options have been forwarded to the transportation department to develop initial potential costs, while the central office team looks more deeply into the impact of Schools of Choice draw-down at specific schools, actual enrollment in fall 2018, potential grandfathering procedures based on past practice, additional "neighborhood adjacent" options, and potential impact to Troy Schools beyond enrollment. An update will be provided at a future Board workshop, with final recommendations to be considered for implementation in the 2019-2020 school year.

Read together, the April 2018 packet is a pause between two heavy meetings: no business items at all, a budget amendment that adds $1,775,565 of revenue and stands up the Early Childhood Learning Center Fund at $2,421,731 for the first time, and a facilities report that names the district's structural attendance problems without yet proposing a fix — while the March minutes carried in the same packet record that the Board's 4-2 divisions over the Section 1 land and the early childhood project were not incidental but consistent.
